query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coating, such as an equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy, when applied to a copper matrix, will significantly enhance its wear resistance and surface protection.
generation.material_initial_state: A copper (Cu) matrix that exhibits comparatively low wear resistance and high susceptibility to surface degradation under mechanical and thermal stress.
generation.intervention: Apply a refractory HEA coating (e.g., NbMoTaW) onto the Cu surface via a deposition technique (such as laser cladding or sputter deposition).
generation.conditions: Testing under high-temperature or high-wear conditions where oxidation or mechanical abrasion is critical to performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The adherent coating layer establishes a robust interface with the Cu substrate. This interface mediates stress transfer and forms a continuous, hard protective barrier.
generation.mechanism: The superior hardness, thermal stability, and formation of protective oxide films (under high-temperature conditions) provided by the refractory HEA inhibit direct wear and slow down oxidation. This ‘barrier effect’ reduces the mechanical degradation of the softer Cu substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated Cu sample is expected to exhibit a lower wear rate and improved retention of surface integrity compared to uncoated Cu, even under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
generation.baseline: Uncoated Cu matrix, which under similar conditions would wear faster and oxidize more readily.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected to hold true as long as the coating adheres well and the thermal expansion mismatch between the HEA and Cu does not induce delamination or interfacial defects during service.
generation.uncertainty: The precise adhesion quality and long-term interfacial stability under extreme thermal cycling remain uncertain; optimization of deposition parameters might be needed to ensure a defect-free and durable interface.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Cu samples, half of which receive the refractory HEA (NbMoTaW) coating using a controlled deposition process, and maintain the other half as uncoated controls. Subject both groups to standardized wear tests (e.g., pin-on-disk) and accelerated high-temperature oxidation cycles.
measurements: Wear rate (mass or volume loss) over a set number of cycles
Adhesion strength of the coating (e.g., via scratch tests)
Microstructural integrity at the interface (e.g., via electron microscopy)
Oxide layer formation and composition (e.g., via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-coated Cu does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and improved oxidation resistance compared to the uncoated Cu under identical test conditions, or if the coating delaminates rapidly under thermal cycling, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use.
